value.overview: The Least Storm-Petrel is a tiny ocean-going seabird and one of the smallest members of the storm-petrel group. It breeds on rocky islands off western Mexico and spends most of its life far from land. With rapid wingbeats, dark plumage, and a low, fluttering flight over waves, it can be difficult to detect. Outside the breeding season, it moves through the tropical and subtropical eastern Pacific, including offshore waters near Central America and Costa Rica.
value.classification: The Least Storm-Petrel belongs to the order Procellariiformes and family Hydrobatidae. Its accepted scientific name is Hydrobates microsoma; older literature may use Oceanodroma microsoma or Halocyptena microsoma.
value.identification: This is a very small, mostly black or dark brown storm-petrel, about 13–15 cm long with a wingspan near 32 cm. It has relatively short, rounded or wedge-shaped wings and a short, wedge-shaped tail. The flight is fast, fluttering, and low over the sea, often giving the bird a bat-like appearance. Its small size helps distinguish it from larger dark storm-petrels, although identification at sea can be difficult in poor light or rough conditions.
value.rangeHabitat: The Least Storm-Petrel breeds on rocky islands off the Baja California Peninsula and in the Gulf of California, Mexico. Away from colonies it is strictly marine, using warm offshore waters, especially the eastern tropical and subtropical Pacific. In Costa Rica it occurs as an uncommon migrant or non-breeding visitor, mainly offshore rather than over land. Records include Pacific waters associated with Costa Rica and surveys around Cocos Island, so it is most likely to be encountered during pelagic trips or offshore research.
value.migrationStatus: Migratory. After breeding in western Mexico, it disperses south through the eastern Pacific; in Costa Rica it is an uncommon offshore migrant and non-breeding visitor, with sightings apparently concentrated in marine waters rather than along the mainland coast.
value.breeding: Breeding colonies are located on remote rocky islands off western Mexico. Pairs nest in rock crevices, among boulder piles, or in other protected cavities, generally without constructing a substantial nest. The species lays one white egg, and both adults are believed to share incubation and chick-rearing. Adults visit colonies mainly at night, when they are less exposed to predators. Breeding information remains less detailed than for many other seabirds, partly because colonies are remote and activity is nocturnal.
value.dietFeeding: The diet is not well documented but appears to consist mainly of zooplankton and other very small marine organisms, including tiny crustaceans. Larval spiny lobsters have also been reported as food. The Least Storm-Petrel usually feeds by fluttering low over the water and picking prey from the surface, rather than diving deeply. It may associate with other seabirds where plankton or other prey become concentrated.
value.behavior: This storm-petrel spends most of its time at sea and is an agile, low-flying bird. Its rapid, deep wingbeats and erratic movements help it maneuver close to wave surfaces. It usually rests and feeds far offshore, making it difficult to observe from land. Like other storm-petrels, it is strongly tied to darkness at breeding colonies, where adults enter crevices and communicate with soft whirring, twittering, or squeaking calls.

conservation.populationTrend: Probably stable overall, although monitoring is limited and population estimates and long-term trend data are uncertain.
